title: Background Jobs and Task Queues
learning_outcomes: Describe Job producers and workers and explain how it relates to Background Jobs and Task Queues.
Demonstrate Queues and job states in a small Node.js example and predict the observable result.
Test a failure, boundary, lifecycle, or version-compatibility case involving Retries.

content.intro: Background Jobs and Task Queues is part of real time systems workers and background jobs. This lesson connects Job producers and workers, Queues and job states, Retries to a concrete Node.js example. Focus on the behavior you can observe, the assumptions the API makes, and one failure or boundary case.
content.why_it_matters: Real-time systems keep connections or background work alive and must manage lifecycle, backpressure, retry, and identity. Test reconnects, duplicate messages, disconnect cleanup, worker failures, and shutdown while work is active.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Real-time systems keep connections or background work alive and must manage lifecycle, backpressure, retry, and identity. Authenticate connections, authorize each event/resource, clean up disconnected clients, and design idempotent job handling.

items.title: Idempotent task execution
items.text: Retries need a finite limit, backoff, jitter, and a clear retryable-error policy. Use idempotency for operations that could otherwise create duplicate effects.

content_blocks.code:
function shouldRetry(attempt, maxAttempts) { return attempt < maxAttempts; }
console.log(shouldRetry(2, 3));
content_blocks.expected_output: true; retries should be bounded and safe operations should be idempotent.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety note
content_blocks.text: Teaching baseline: use a supported Node.js LTS release (Node.js 24 LTS as checked on 2026-10-13). The official releases page lists Node.js 26 as Current and Node.js 24/22 as LTS. Some advanced APIs, flags, permission behavior, embedded SQLite capabilities, module-loader hooks, and TypeScript integration are version-sensitive; verify the exact installed runtime. The Node.js 22 runtime available in the build-check environment is used only for syntax checks. This example is for learning and static validation, not for executing untrusted learner code inside CodeLeaf.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a socket connection itself proves the caller can access every message or resource.
common_mistakes.why: The code may pass a simple demonstration yet fail with real inputs, resource limits, timing, or runtime differences.
common_mistakes.fix: Apply authorization at the event/resource boundary and persist critical work with explicit idempotency keys.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a snippet without checking its runtime, dependencies, input assumptions, or cleanup behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Node.js APIs and surrounding ecosystem tools have explicit version, trust, and resource boundaries.
common_mistakes.fix: State the environment and dependency assumptions, then rerun the example from a clean starting state.
